_comment: Recorded measurements for the GR00T N1.7 fine-tuning stage. Every number in the stage
README, the figures and the report is derived from this file, so the analysis reproduces
without a GPU: `python3 analyze.py`.
Evaluation protocol is identical across every row unless stated: task
galileo_g1_static_pick_and_place (apple -> plate), embodiment g1_wbc_agile_joint_brainco,
50 Hz, 14 s episode timeout, success = the environment's own termination term. Where the
spawn jitter differs it is recorded per row, because it is not comparable across values.
`n` is pooled across repeat runs of the same configuration; `runs` lists the parts.

protocol.success_caveat: the term also counts the apple being pushed into the region, so it is an upper bound on true pick-and-place

datasets.label:
Rounds 1-2
(uniform jitter)
datasets.why: First scale-up. Mimic replays the harvested successes over an apple spawn jittered uniformly in a narrow box around the nominal pose.

datasets.label:
Round 3
(targeted hard cells)
datasets.why: Added only where the r1r2 policy failed. The spawn box was gridded, per-cell success measured, and generation aimed at the weak cells instead of sampling uniformly again.

datasets.label: Merged r2+r3
datasets.why: Union of the two, used for the second fine-tune. 2647 = 1668 + 979 and 1304904 = 821610 + 483294, so nothing was dropped in the merge.

_comment: Apple spawn position vs success. This is the analysis that decided round 3, and the one that
in hindsight also explains why round 3 could not work.
Raw data is in spawn_eval.csv (99 evaluation episodes of ft_r1r2 checkpoint-5000 at +/-5 cm,
with the spawn offset and outcome of each) and spawn_demos.csv (the spawn offset of all 1668
r1r2 training demonstrations). analyze.py bins both onto the 3x3 grid below, so the per-cell
numbers here are derived rather than asserted -- they are recorded for reference only.
Axis convention: x is reach away from the robot, y is away from the plate, both cm from the
nominal spawn. Evaluation offsets are centred on the run's own mean, which cancels the
constant bias in the pixel-to-world homography used to recover them; demonstration offsets
are taken from the nominal pose directly. Homography noise is about +/-1 cm, so cell
boundaries are approximate.
THE THREE QUANTITIES, and the point of comparing them:
sim success        varies 6x across the box (0.17 to 1.00) -- the thing we care about
offline action MSE varies 1.4x (1.27 to 1.77 e-3) with no spatial structure at all
demos per cell     varies 1.2x (165 to 199) -- essentially uniform coverage
So the weak cells were neither under-represented in the data nor flagged by the model's own
imitation error. Round 3 targeted the success map, which was the right map to target, but
the premise that adding demonstrations would fix those cells was wrong: they already had the
same number of demonstrations as the cells scoring 1.00.
Mean action MSE of the same checkpoint replayed offline against 400 held-out dataset
episodes at their exact recorded spawns -- no homography noise, and cheap compared to a
rollout. The hope was that it would reproduce the success map for a fraction of the cost.
It does not: spread is 1.4x against success's 6x, correlation with distance from centre is
-0.06 and with y is +0.03, and cell-wise correlation with sim success is -0.24 over 8
cells, which is noise at that n. The offline metric is spatially blind and must not be used
for targeting.
Unlike every other number in this file these cannot be recomputed from the CSVs -- they
need the model and a GPU -- so they are transcribed from that run, in units of 1e-3.
Rows are the x bands in cell_edges_cm order, columns the y bands.
The same disagreement along the training axis rather than the spatial one: offline MSE
improves monotonically with training while sim success does not move. Another reason this
work is evaluated by rollout only.
plan_targeted.py: weight = Beta(1,1) posterior mean failure rate per cell, zeroed for
cells already above 0.70 success or with fewer than 3 eval episodes, then normalised to a
1000-demo budget. 979 were actually generated. Keyed by [x_band, y_band] index.

regrasp_audit._comment: Counts hand-close events per episode on action dim 23 (left_hand, the only actuated hand in this task). The command is binary: 0.0 open, -0.87 rad closed. A retry would appear as >= 2 close events.

Revo2 hands, frozen policy
(retargeting only)
evals.note: all six frame-verified as genuine grasps; the gap fine-tuning had to close

evals.label: Revo2, fine-tuned on r1r2
note: NOT REPORTED, and the reason is the point. This is the fine-tuned checkpoint evaluated at
the single fixed spawn pose the stock task ships with -- which is the pose every one of its
1,668 training demonstrations was generated around. Asking a policy that has seen one apple
position hundreds of times for that exact position again tests it on its own training point,
so 19/20 measures memorisation of one pose rather than the skill the fine-tune was meant to
buy. Kept for provenance, deliberately excluded from every figure and every claim. The
reportable fine-tuned number is ft_r1r2_c5000, at +/-5 cm.
The two frozen rows sit at the same fixed pose, but nothing was fitted to it in their case,
so for them it is simply the task as shipped.

evals.label: fine-tuned r1r2, +/-10 cm
evals.note: collapses outside the training spawn box; this is what motivated round 3

_comment: Does the failure mode live in how the chunk is executed, rather than in the weights?
The policy predicts 40 actions (0.8 s at 50 Hz). Stock executes all 40 before looking at the
world again. Three alternatives were tried, all on the same checkpoint and protocol.
None produced a retry after a failed grasp, which is the behaviour being chased.

hard_swap_early_test._comment: The first attempt, run earlier on the r1r2 checkpoint: shorten the executed chunk and replace it outright.

failure_analysis._comment: Per-episode outcome for the two pooled stock runs on the final checkpoint. Frames at 50 Hz; 700 frames is the 14 s timeout.
